title: Doughnuts, Economics & Humanitarianism?
html:
A couple years ago, I stumbled upon something called Doughnut Economics and asked myself the same question you might be asking: what do doughnuts have to do with economics? I read some of the information available online and became interested in how this emerging model may intersect with disaster response and how it can or will be enabled by technology.

I kept the idea in the back of my mind until this past summer when Sarah A Jabbar joined me and expressed a similar interest. We were not sure if there would be any real connection with the humanitarian & technology intersection but we were keen to explore it. Why? Perhaps that is best answered by Paula Gil Baizan, from NRC Innovation, who noted in Trumanitarian episode 15 that, in order to be innovative, the humanitarian sector should be watching what is going on in the fringes. And, one of the examples she pointed out was the Doughnut Model of Economics!

Being a relatively new economic model, the amount of information and number of implementations to review were limited. Being able to chat with people like Kate Raworth, the creator of the model, to review information from actual implementations like in Amsterdam, to learn about the growing network of cities and nations exploring the possibility of implementation, and to read articles from skeptics, gave us a good understanding of the concept.

We have compiled our notes and finding into a short report: About Doughnut Economics, Technology and Humanitarian Crises - October 2021

[PDF]

As you might expect, our report does not have any grand reveal. There are no major shocks or declarations. But, it does make you start to think about humanitarian response in a more sustainable or balanced way. Or simply raise questions for responders such as: How can we adjust our response to a location that has adopted such a model? How can we deliver aid in accordance with the underlying principles of this model even if the affected area uses a more traditional economic model? How can we better power the circular economy and support organizations like Rightboot who help solve problems that need to be addressed in order to balance the doughnut. Listen to Trumanitarian Episode 32 to learn more about Rightboot.

And, the technology-related extension for me becomes: How can technology support the model’s implementation? How does it enable organizations to change to a new reality? How does it enable new and innovative organizations to get off the ground? Of course the internet enables the spread of lessons learned. But how will things like better/faster data, machine learning, dashboards, SaaS and No-Code tools, etc., help make an implementation (more) successful?

Perhaps it is just food for thought at this moment. But, I suspect that a time will soon come when we need to adjust our delivery to match such a modern model.

Andrej
teaser: Notes with Sarah A Jabbar on Doughnut Economics and how a modern delivery model might affect humanitarian work.
